content: The information provided highlights the importance of monitoring antiretroviral (ARV) drug toxicities and their impact on patient outcomes. This data is critical for developing strategies to prevent and mitigate drug toxicity, optimize patient management, and improve retention and viral suppression rates during treatment. The 2020 WHO guidelines recommend collecting data on programmatic reasons for switching antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens or treatment interruptions, defined as the percentage of individuals on ART who switch or stop their ARV regimen. In 2020, WHO also recommended specific indicators to monitor the safety of ARV drugs during pregnancy. These include the proportion of low birth weight deliveries (<2.5 kg) among HIV-positive women, the proportion of stillbirths or miscarriages, the proportion of preterm deliveries (<37 weeks gestation), and the proportion of HIV-positive women with first-trimester ART exposure associated with major congenital anomalies. A higher-than-expected rate of adverse pregnancy outcomes on these indicators necessitates further formal assessments, such as birth defect surveillance or pregnancy registries. Longitudinal monitoring is essential to address emerging concerns and risk factors related to ARV drug toxicity. WHO recommends that countries implement longitudinal monitoring of people living with HIV to track changes in body weight or body mass index, screen for ARV toxicity risk factors, and assess the impact of ARVs on metabolic comorbidities, cardiovascular disease, and maternal and pregnancy outcomes. This approach complements adverse drug reaction reporting by utilizing clinical data from HIV patient monitoring systems to identify patterns in adverse drug reactions or risk factors over time. The feasibility of longitudinal monitoring depends on the availability of electronic medical records (EMRs). Data can be extracted, anonymized, and analyzed periodically at selected sites to inform clinical practice at the national level. Key data elements for longitudinal monitoring include weight gain, patient demographics, medical history, clinical characteristics, comorbidities, risk factors associated with weight gain, and drug exposure details. Early warning indicators (EWIs) of HIV drug resistance are a set of quality-of-care indicators used to evaluate whether ART programs deliver services of sufficient quality to minimize the emergence of HIV drug resistance. Monitoring EWIs helps identify gaps in service delivery that can be addressed to reduce resistance risk and optimize program performance. Findings from EWI monitoring can guide resource allocation to clinics most in need of support and address critical gaps in service delivery. Factors contributing to HIV drug resistance or viral non-suppression include viral factors (e.g., subtype, replication capacity, pre-existing polymorphisms), drug-related factors (e.g., potency, pharmacokinetics, drug-drug interactions, tolerability, genetic barriers to resistance), and programmatic factors (e.g., adherence, drug stock-outs, patient attrition, and viral load testing). Monitoring programmatic factors can alert ART programs to situations that may favor the emergence of resistance or virological failure at the population level. WHO recommends that EWIs be reported on a census of patients where resources and data quality are adequate. Where this is not feasible, EWIs can be reported on a nationally representative sample of patients or collected separately by clinics, depending on the country context. Resources should focus on strengthening routine patient monitoring systems rather than creating parallel systems for EWI data collection and reporting. Data quality gaps should be addressed promptly, and weaknesses in reported data should be noted to facilitate interpretation of indicators. For pediatric populations, monitoring includes general and HIV-specific indicators. Age disaggregation in five-year intervals is important, as interventions may vary by age. Key general child health monitoring includes growth monitoring, developmental assessments, immunizations, and infant feeding practices in the context of HIV. Infants exposed to HIV may be identified early if the mother receives services for prevention of vertical transmission or late if identified outside the cascade of interventions. Infants identified as exposed during pregnancy or postpartum may be classified as high or low risk for HIV transmission based on maternal ART use and viral suppression. Postnatal prophylaxis is provided accordingly, with single or dual ARVs for six weeks for low-risk infants and extended prophylaxis for high-risk infants. Late-identified infants may receive presumptive treatment with triple ARVs. If HIV infection is ruled out, postnatal prophylaxis is provided as for high-risk infants. If infection is confirmed, presumptive treatment transitions to recommended first-line ART. Key indicators for monitoring include postnatal prophylaxis coverage, co-trimoxazole coverage, timing and duration of vertical transmission, antenatal and postnatal care attendance, maternal HIV testing and re-testing coverage, maternal ART coverage during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and maternal viral suppression during these periods. For children living with HIV, monitoring the transition to optimized ART regimens, such as dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens for children >20 kg and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPVr) or DTG for children <20 kg, is critical. As DTG becomes more widely available, transitioning children previously optimized to LPVr to pediatric DTG should also be monitored. Treatment monitoring should follow the WHO-recommended viral load algorithm, and access to psychosocial support for adherence should be assessed.
